content.comment_body: Hello, I have a [product_name] with firmware [version_no] connected to a [product_name] operator panel. Everything generally works, but the controller randomly loses its user program. When I check the controller, the program has stopped; attempting to start it displays 'Empty program,' so I need to reload it with my laptop. Any advice would be appreciated.

This situation shouldn't normally occur. When you download the program from your PC to the [product_name] controller, it gets stored in flash memory, which is resistant to power outages. I have several controllers from the [article_no] series and none have lost their program during a power loss. Could you clarify your procedure? Are you using an SD card for the program storage?

I set up a network project using [product_name] engineering software that includes one controller and one HMI. I created a new circuit, downloaded it to the controller over the network, and made the HMI program with [product_name] engineering tool before downloading it to the panel. I'm not using an SD card for the program. There were no issues during extended home testing, but now, after installing onsite, the controller lost its program twice within 24 hours. I plan to try disconnecting the HMI next week to help isolate the issue.

I've never encountered a situation where this type of controller loses its program. As mentioned, programs are stored in flash memory, which resists power loss, so the program shouldn't disappear. If you are truly losing the user program, the controller may be malfunctioning, though I doubt that's the case. Alternatively, is it possible only setpoints or values are resetting, rather than the entire program?

Hello, you're focusing on the idea that the HMI causes this problem—is there a specific reason for this suspicion? If you have solid evidence, it's best to reach out to [company_name] support using their request link. However, I have reasonable doubts that the HMI is responsible. Is it possible someone deliberately deletes the program? Accessing the controller’s internal screen allows this if admin mode—which is enabled by default—is active, so setting the unit to operator mode helps secure the device. Can anyone currently access admin mode on your device? Also, be sure to set your own passwords to protect the controller.

I found a forum thread suggesting the operator panel could be causing issues: [url]. I've used these controllers for years and never had this happen before, and this is my first time connecting an operator panel to one. While reviewing help files, I noticed a note about connecting devices using S7 or Modbus protocols; I had enabled both for Ethernet, but now I switched to S7 only and will monitor if it helps. If not, I'll disconnect the panel to check if the problem persists.
Could you clarify your situation? Do you truly believe the entire program is getting lost, or is it only operational values such as setpoints that disappear?
In the related forum topic, it's unclear whether the user program is actually lost. The usual issue with operator panels is the loss of setpoints after power failure.

That's not typically a problem when using an operator panel. As another user suggested, initiate a support request. If the controller loses its program—and no one has deleted it—it may be defective, although this is a rare issue.

Hi, this case can be referred to [company_name] support for detailed assistance free of charge. Please review your profile area under 'My Forum' for individual support options. Regards, [product_name] Support

I've disconnected the operator panel to see if the issue persists. Considering replacing the power supply as well. The controller lost its program twice in five days, including while I was present in the control panel; I noticed a malfunctioning light and discovered the program had stopped, and when attempting to start, received the error message. I'll contact support if it happens again.

The controller lost its program again today. Support suggested if there is an SD card installed in the controller without a program, powering up may overwrite the user program with an empty one. Not sure if this applies—I’ve had an SD card installed for data logging for a month with no issues until now. The controller loses power nightly, and there’s no binary program file on the SD card. I’ve reinstalled the program onto both the controller and SD card to monitor further. If it happens again, I’ll consider replacing the controller. Any additional recommendations are welcome.

1) I haven't heard of other users facing your issue. 2) It's unlikely related to the operator panel. 3) If there isn't an empty program file on the SD card, the controller can't load an empty program. 4) Are you certain no one is deleting the program? Change the password for switching between operator and admin modes (the default is known), and keep the controller in operator mode for security. Only in admin mode can the device be switched to STOP; if running, no one can delete the program.

The controller is currently set to operator mode, but I haven't changed the password yet. I'll do so on my next site visit. It seems advisable to keep a copy of the program on the SD card at all times.

There's no issue if the latest program version is on the SD card. On every restart, the controller reads the program from the SD card and loads it into memory. If you modify the program, remember to update the SD card accordingly.

analysis.insight_summary: Forum members report unexpected loss of the user program in a [product_name] controller after integrating it with a [product_name] operator panel. The underlying reason is unclear, with attention on connections and protocol settings, such as S7 versus Modbus on Ethernet. This causes operational disruption, as the device displays 'Empty program' and requires manual reloading. Experienced members note this is abnormal, as these controllers should retain user programs through power cycles and voltage failures.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect the [product_name] controller to reliably keep user programs during operation and after power interruptions, even when connected to operator panels. They want consistent, dependable performance without losing programs unexpectedly.
